timeline: What happens when you drop a 13th-century temple brick into a pool of water and watch it float instead of sinking?
Built in 1213 by the Kakatiya general Recherla Rudra, the shrine uses porous bricks made from clay, resinous gum, jute fiber, and rice husks.
When fired in kilns, the organic gum burned away, leaving tiny air pockets that dropped the density below water.
This ingenious weight reduction protected the soaring five-storied vimana tower from collapsing during severe earthquakes.
Beneath the stone floors, a massive sandbox foundation absorbed seismic shockwaves across eight centuries.
Surviving Malik Kafur's violent invasion in thirteen ten, the temple remains an engineering marvel of medieval India.
UNESCO recognized this architectural triumph as a World Heritage Site in twenty twenty-one.
Even today, the floating bricks of the Ramappa Temple challenge everything we know about ancient masonry.
You can test the floating bricks of the Ramappa Temple yourself, as these 13th-century clay blocks defy conventional weight.
